speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: O.E.C.D.-REPORT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON SIGNING OF CONVENTION IN PARIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to offer the house a report on the successful outcome of the meeting held in Paris on December 13 and 14 to consider and sign a convention under which the organization for economic co-operation and development is to be established next year.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) and I represented the government and signed the convention on behalf of Canada. Other representatives signed on behalf of Austria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the three European communities; that is to say, the coal and steel community, the atomic energy community and the European economic community. It is the intention of the government to seek parliamentary approval of the convention at this session.
On January 18 last I made a report to the house on the events that had led to the establishment in 1948 of the organization for European economic co-operation in connection with the Marshall plan, to the subsequent associate membership of Canada and the United States in that organization in 1950, and to the recent decision to reconstitute the organization to meet the needs of the future 90205-6-55i
and to provide for the full membership of these two countries. It is gratifying to be able, less than a year later, to report to the house that the task of reconstitution has been accomplished, subject to the necessary processes of ratification.
Negotiations have proceeded very actively throughout the past year. In July a second ministerial meeting was held in Paris in order to give guidance and direction to the negotiators. My report on that meeting was read to the house by my parliamentary secretary on July 25.
The aims of the newly constituted organization, as set forth in article 1 of the convention, are to promote policies that are designed: (a) to achieve the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries, while maintaining financial stability and thus to contribute to the development of the world economy; (b) to contribute to sound economic expansion in member as well as non-member countries in the process of economic development; and (c) to contribute to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral non-discriminatory basis in accordance with international obligations.
The activities of the organization may be broadly classified under three heads: trade, aid', and the harmonization of the economic policies of member governments. Of these the third is the least familiar but it might well emerge as the most important. Therefore I should like to speak of it first.
In the field of economic policy there is growing recognition of international interdependence. National economies have become more sensitive to changes in world trends and to measures taken in other countries. Actions taken by individual governments often have external repercussions and, indeed, the efficacy of national action is to a large extent dependent upon the policies followed in other countries. Accordingly it has been agreed that in the new organization the economic and financial situation in member countries and policies pursued by member governments will be kept under review. Special attention will be paid to the international effects of national policies. And, as set out in the convention, member countries have undertaken to pursue, both individually and jointly, "policies designed to achieve economic growth and internal and external financial stability

Report on Paris Trade Convention and to avoid developments which might endanger their economies or those of other countries".
Similarly, in the field of trade member countries agree to review together their general policies and practices and to devote special attention to the international effects of their actions. The organization will provide a continuing forum for consideration of the effects, on member countries and on others, of the trade groupings that are emerging in Europe. I refer, of course, to issues arising from the formation of the Six and the Seven. Such matters as these are of concern currently and for the future. On the other hand, it has been decided that much of the earlier activity of the O.E.E.C. in the field of trade, which was of a regional character and often discriminated against the rest of the world, should be discontinued. The new organization is, as I have said, to promote the expansion of trade on a multilateral and non-discriminatory basis, thus contributing to the achievement of the purposes of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
Turning finally to the field of aid, it should be explained that the existing organization, the O.E.E.C., is already engaged in useful programs of technical assistance in the less fully developed countries amongst its own membership; these are countries bordering the Mediterranean sea. Such programs may be expected to continue. However, the organization also includes the most fully industrialized countries of the world and, under the new constitution, these countries are recognizing a responsibility for aid not only to their less advanced neighbours and associates but also to underdeveloped countries throughout the world. Without awaiting the new constitution, the chief aid-providing countries of Europe, along with representatives of Japan, have already during the course of the past year held three meetings, two in Washington and one in Bonn. This group is to become the development aid committee of the new organization. Its purpose is to promote, by means of consultation and harmonization, an improved flow of aid to underdeveloped countries.
The new O.E.C.D. provides great hope for the economic future of the free world. The significance of its role will depend on the willingness of all member countries to make their full contribution and, through co-operation and consultation, to ensure effective use of their capacities and potentialities, and to promote the highest sustainable growth of their economies and those of other countries. It will be the intention of the Canadian
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) .1

government to make the organization an effective instrument for the betterment of our own people and of people throughout the world.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to table copies in English and in French of the convention and the communique issued at the time it was approved for signature, and copies in both languages of the statement which I made on behalf of Canada, partly in French and partly in English, at the signing ceremony at the Quai d'Orsay on Wednesday, December 14.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-REPORT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON SIGNING OF CONVENTION IN PARIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the minister back from his short visit to Europe; and his close friends, among whom I propose to include myself, regret that on his return to Canada he did not take advantage of the festivities participated in yesterday in Montreal by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The minister has given us a review of the organization known as O.E.C.D., the organization for European co-operation and development. It is perhaps sufficient to say at this time that until the convention has been tabled and we have been given an opportunity of examining in detail its contents it would be wise to perhaps no more than note that this organization, a successor to the O.E.E.C., is a step in the right direction. Obviously in the new organization Canada and the United States will have a more active role in relation to the formation of the two new economic blocs in Europe and the European nations generally than we had in O.E.E.C. Undoubtedly the new organization about which the minister has reported to the house owes its existence primarily to the initiative and the leadership of the United States, in which Mr. Dillon of that country played a notable part.
The minister said nothing about the free trade association under the leadership of the United Kingdom in Europe, nor of the E.C.M., or the European common market, in connection with which O.E.C.D. will have, of course, an important part to play. We will reserve our full judgment on this matter until such time as we have seen the convention in full context. We hope that it will be possible for the government to reconcile its adhesion to the convention with the observations made by the Minister of Finance a few weeks ago when he was in England, and which made extremely difficult any contact or association by the United Kingdom with the formation of one of the European economic blocs, something that means so much not only to the people of Europe but to the peace of the world.

maintopic: O.E.C.D.-REPORT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON SIGNING OF CONVENTION IN PARIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all welcome the return of the Minister of Finance, and listened to him with a great deal of interest. 1 think it can be said that the initiative and the impetus given to this conference and its conclusion have come about not particularly because of action of the North American nations but because of the success that is attending the setting up of the European common market and the outer seven, and the dangers and the advantages that flow from this action to other parts of the world.
More than any other nation, perhaps, Canada has a great stake in such a successful arrangement of nations to meet these great problems. Canada's life depends to a large extent upon a successful export trade. The O.E.C.D., properly managed, I believe can bring about great benefit to the Canadian nation. We hope that this move is but another indication of the growing community of world nations, another indication that nations in the world can co-operate for their mutual advantage. In any effort the government puts forward to extend Canadian trade through this organization and others I am sure it will receive the support of the members of the house.

Mr. Speaker, during the past few days there has been considerable discussion about trade with Cuba, and I should like to clarify some of the points that have been raised.
Yesterday a request was made that copies should be tabled of the seventeen export permits which have been issued since October 1, 1960, for shipments to Cuba. I should like to make it clear that I would have no objection whatever to the tabling of these permits in this instance if it were not for the fact that, as a matter of principle, it has been the consistent practice of this government and of the preceding government to respect the confidential nature of the information which must be disclosed by firms applying for export permits. We do not intend to depart from this practice.
Having said that, let me go as far as I can to reassure the house that this stand is in no way adopted for the purpose of refusing information to the house. Because of the importance of this subject I will go further than I would in normal circumstances consider appropriate, and without in any way committing myself to follow a similar course by such a precedent, advise the type of goods which were export licensed. All but five of the permits issued were to cover supply to
Statement on Cuban Trade the Cubana Airlines of parts and instruments and reserviced engines which initially had been sent to Canada from Cuba for repairs. These were for the Viscount and Britannia aircraft operated by Cubana Airlines. The other items include part of a cobalt therapy unit, some rebuilt automobile transmissions, some rock drilling supplies, and parts for radio sets. I can assure the house that no application has been received for a permit to export goods of a strategic significance to Cuba.
There was some confusion apparent in yesterday's debate on the part of certain hon. members regarding what might be defined as strategic materials. The acting minister referred to the range and variety of products which are on the export control list. The export control list incorporates materials which are classified as strategic by COCOM, the co-ordinating committee in Paris, in which agreement on strategic items is developed among NATO governments. The list includes arms and ammunition, military and related equipment, and raw materials which are of strategic significance. No permits have been, or will be, issued for export of these goods to Cuba.
It also includes materials under control for supply conservation purposes, such as logs, iron and steel scrap, pancreas glands, and so on. There are items on the export control list which in some circumstances have strategic significance, but in other circumstances, none. For example, aircraft engines might have strategic significance if they were for military operational aircraft, but not if they were for ordinary civilian aircraft. Aircraft engines are subject to strict permit control, and the circumstances in each case will govern whether or not there is any strategic significance to an export and, accordingly, whether or not a permit is issued.
As the Prime Minister stated, in our trade relations with Cuba, consideration is given at all times to the strategic nature of any goods involved, and no permits have been issued this year for equipment which may be regarded as having any strategic significance.
As the Prime Minister has also stated, there is no intention of permitting what, in effect, would amount to bootlegging of goods of United States origin to Cuba. To implement this policy, no permits will be issued for the re-export of United States origin goods to Cuba.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce my department's intention to provide financial assistance to the Canadian Olympic association in studies it is conducting in connection with the 1968 winter Olympic games.
The association has requested a grant of $10,000 to finance an engineering survey of the most probable sites in this country, to determine which site would give Canada the best opportunity for selection as the host country for these games. I was pleased to accede to the association's request, and hope

that parliament will give its approval if it should be necessary to include this item in final supplementary estimates for the current year.
The Canadian Olympic association hopes to make a definite choice at its annual meeting in March, 1961, after a report from its consultants has been received. The final choice as to the host country will be made by the international Olympic committee in 1963. However, it is most important that one Canadian site should be settled upon as quickly as possible, in order that the financial aspects and conditions of eligibility may be considered in advance by all the parties concerned.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, December 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Starr for the third reading of Bill No. C-52, to establish a national productivity council.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rose last night a few minutes before the house concluded its deliberations for the day to explain why the official opposition intended, notwithstanding the rejection by the house of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), to vote for third reading of this bill.
I was asked by the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Martineau) if I would explain to the house how I could justify voting for this bill after describing it as a farce. I believe the whole debate on both sides of the house has shown that, as a measure to deal with the present unemployment problem, this bill is a farce. If there had been any doubt about it, that doubt surely was resolved when the vote was taken on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex East and the house rejected that amendment which would have included among the purposes and objects of this council the promotion of employment.
Now, the rejection of that motion was a decision by the house-and a similar decision had been made previously in committee-to the effect that the promotion of employment was not an object of this measure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is just nonsense.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister, who is an authority on the subject, says this is nonsense. No greater authority on that subject, I think, exists. Since the Prime Minister was absent from the house at the time, I shall

Productivity Council
read to him what was said by the Minister of Labour when he rejected the amendment I moved in committee. These remarks will be found at page 832 of yesterday's Hansard.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Before the hon. member proceeds, does he not think that since the house has voted on the question of including among the powers of the council the promotion of employment, that subject has been determined by a vote of the house in so far as it relates to the council and its powers, and therefore should not be taken up again when we are on the motion for third reading?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think there is a good deal in Your Honour's contention, but since the Prime Minister has interjected and described a bald statement of fact as nonsense I feel, in view of the latitude that has been allowed to other hon. members in this debate,
I should be allowed to quote the precise words of the minister in rejecting the amendment. This is all I propose to do, and I do not intend to go beyond that. These remarks are reported on page 832 of Hansard for December 15, 1960:
The purpose of this productivity council is to bring about increased efficiency in the productivity of industry. Because of that, naturally, employment will be created to a greater degree.
Then follow really the important words.
The effect of this amendment would be that the council would he dealing directly with the employment or unemployment factor. That is not to be the case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Go ahead and finish the statement.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has asked me to go ahead and finish the statement, and I am very happy to do that because, unlike some hon. gentlemen, I do not like to denature other people's words. I shall come to that in a moment.
That is not to be the case. This council will be dealing with the efficiency of productivity in industry, and employment will be a natural consequence of its work.
It is our view that employment will not be a natural consequence of the work of the council. We expressed that view over and over again in the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: You hope it will not be.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I say, and it has been said by many other hon. members and at one stage of the debate it was even implied by the Minister of Labour himself, that increases in productivity very often have the effect of making workers redundant and creating unemployment; that is our position. Our disappointment over this bill is precisely because it did not do what we thought it would do before it was introduced, and what the Leader of the Opposition indicated

as much as two years ago should be done. We believe that a study of automation should be made with a view to dealing with an urgent problem, the problem of finding alternative employment for redundant workers.
I should like now to reply to the question asked by the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister. Why, in that case, do we vote for this bill at all? I must say that is a very good question to be asked, because what this council is likely to accomplish in the light of the arguments put forward by its sponsor, its godfather and its stepfather is so confused, so uncertain, that I do not believe we could be blamed very much if we raised some questions as to whether or not it would be worth even the $150,000 a year it is going to cost. However, if we can get 100 men employed for a whole year or even 50 men employed for a whole year, and if we can bring about some increase in productivity at the same time, I would think perhaps a gamble with that $150,000 would not be, in the circumstances, unjustified.
Moreover, as everyone who has spoken on this side of the house has said-the hon. member for Ottawa West, the hon. member for Niagara Falls, and every other person on this side af the house-the long term objective of increasing productivity, in the kind of world in which we live, is a good thing. If this bill had been introduced later in the session, not under false pretences but simply to deal with that problem, a lot of the debate that has taken place now would not have taken place. At any rate, it seems to me that there is no reason for voting against it and, by itself-

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is pretty weak.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Well, the hon. member says that is pretty weak. What kind of argument can you give but a weak argument for voting for this weak bill? The second reason is that the Minister of Labour told us that this council was going to show some results in terms of employment in six months, or by June 14. We might be wrong and he might be right.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: You are wrong.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We shall find out next June. We are not going to stop anything that might have that effect, even though we are extremely sceptical about it.
The third reason is that we feel there is an economic emergency with respect to unemployment when 429,000 people, an increase of 61,000 between October and November, are unemployed this early in the winter.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
And there are
more now.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We think there is an economic emergency even it the government does not think so. We recognize the fact that the government and not the opposition has the responsibility and the power to act, and that the government alone has that power. We believe that a responsible opposition should not thwart government policies to deal with unemployment unless we think they are positively harmful. We do not think this measure is positively harmful. We feel that the government should be given a chance to get this law on the statute books, to set up this council and to show that we were wrong. However, that feeling does not alter our duty as a responsible opposition to point out our scepticism about it; and I may say that our scepticism is, as we have all indicated, very great indeed.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I say this, and perhaps I could sum up all the rest of my argument in this way. If we cannot have a loaf or even half a loaf, we are not going to reject a crumb. For that reason we will vote for this bill although we do not consider that it is even an approach to the urgent problem of unemployment. The fact that this is an urgent problem, and an extremely urgent one indeed, I think was underlined by a statement which was made by the hon. member for Assiniboia last evening and which will be found at page 851 of Hansard. The hon. member stated as follows:
-we have a higher rate of unemployment than we had in any time during the last 15 years.
There was some exchange of remarks and I took some exception to that statement. I pointed out that there was not a higher rate 15 years ago, and I was seeking to indicate merely that the dominion bureau of statistics figures on which these figures are based started only 15 years ago and that is why there is this 15-year date. In fact I took the trouble to look the matter up. The fact is that in November of 1945, 3.8 per cent of the labour force was unemployed as compared with 6.6 per cent at this time, notwithstanding the fact that this date was in the middle of demobilization and immediately after the cessation of war production.
I noticed that in another place, namely in Fredericton, on December 10, Saturday evening last-this is from the paper of December 12-the Prime Minister made a speech in honour of the new Minister of Forestry, who is present with us and whom I have not previously had an opportunity to welcome to the house. I think this will apply to hon. members opposite, and while they are listening to me their suspense can mount with regard to further wise observations that can be made, I do not doubt, in answer to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
There is one aspect of that hon. member's frequent interjections in the course of this debate which has puzzled me; that is his references to the paternity of this bill. Sometimes he refers to the father of the bill. At other times he talks about the father in law and, again, at other times he speaks of the stepfather. Well, in view of the amendment which the hon. member proposed, and which was voted down, and in view also of his past prolific record in producing different things, including a famous work of fiction, and including also famous Canadian babies, I think the hon. gentleman is not at all in the position of a father. He is certainly much more in the position of a rejected suitor. Incidentally, someone has just asked "What does that make the baby?" We might as well not get into that aspect of it.
Before the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate spoke, I intended to deal, and I still intend to deal, with some of the more or less serious criticisms which have been directed against this bill. A few minutes ago the hon. member quoted many figures relating to unemployment in past years under Conservative regimes and under Liberal regimes. If I may, I should also like to delve a little into history and refresh the memory of hon. members opposite. Reading from the records we see that on May 15, 1939 the then minister of labour, Mr. Rogers, proposed in the house the following motion-and this was almost four years after the Liberals had taken power-
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress.
Is that not in itself a striking indictment? Is it not a proof, and a very lucid proof, that there then existed, after three and a half years of great Liberal rule, an enormous amount of distress both in industry and in agriculture? During the same debate the minister stated that in those days one lived continually in an atmosphere of distress. He pointed to unemployment as a persistent condition, and well he might have. Here are some of the figures which I should like to quote in order to illustrate in a graphic way the great progress achieved in four years of

Liberal administration from 1935 to 1939. Here are the elements of the story, one by one:
1.	A survey carried out by the Canadian youth congress showed that 465,000' youths between 15 and 30 were not in gainful employment.
2.	In February of 1939, 1,012,000 people were in receipt of direct relief.
Well might the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate have talked a few minutes ago about relief paid by this administration. If he looks at the record he will find that while the Liberals were in power there was a sorry record of direct relief and subsidies being paid out to a suffering Canadian population years after the administration of the late Mr. Mackenzie King had reached power. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred to Right Hon. Mr. Bennett as having perpetrated what he called a fraud upon the Canadian people by saying he would solve the problem of Canadian unemployment. If the hon. member will refer to the campaign of 1935 he will find that the whole appeal of the Liberal party during that campaign was based on a claim that they, the wise Solomons who are now sitting opposite, would solve that problem. But they never did.

I think it is time to forget about who did what in 1930 or 1940. We have only a few days left, and I suggest we should make progress. result of the debates in this chamber; some assurance that something will be done, and done soon.

This is the first time I have entered this debate. I have not spoken on any of the previous stages although I think I am more qualified to speak on this bill than perhaps any hon. member of the opposition who has spoken to date. I wonder how many jobs the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) or the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) have created?
Would you like an answer to that question?

It was a rhetorical question, and I know the answer. It is, none. As a result of my background of industrial engineering I have had the job of setting up plants, of providing employment, of using capital, machines and men in order to build up or make a product which can be sold in the markets of Canada and the world. That is not an easy task, but it would have been easier if we had had the benefit of the facilities which are envisaged in this bill. I would recommend to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that he should visit a little place north of Oshawa where he would see an old barn where Robert McLaughlin built the famous carriages which bore his name. I have seen a picture of the working force there, some 12 men. Out of this group came a corporation with 15,000 employees. This is progress, though it also means unsettlement. The blacksmith lost his job, but 200 metal finishers found jobs.
This present measure is in my opinion one of the most important bills which will be introduced in this or any other parliament, because this bill points the way to co-operation between all sections of the economy and particularly between management and labour in order to construct an economy in Canada which will survive. This represents a means of co-operation by government with labour, with industry and with agriculture. It is something which we are attempting to do and which is already working in Europe, the United Kingdom and in the near and far east where there are over 30 productivity centres which have in fact increased employment, increased production, increased earnings, reduced operating costs and introduced new products, all of which this measure is intended to bring about.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate quoted the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) as saying, on page 832 of Hansard:
This council will be dealing with the efficiency of productivity in industry, and employment will be a natural consequence of its work.

The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate said this was a fiction and a farce, and that employment will not be the natural consequence of the work of this council. I suspect that the hon. member, because of his recent literary efforts, may be called an expert on fiction. Maybe that is the cause of his bias against this word. I suggest he should go to Hong Kong. There he might see women carrying two wicker baskets over their shoulders moving earth. A good front end loader would take the place of 20 or 30 of them. This is the type of thinking which typifies the hon. member. It is rickshaw thinking, and rickety rickshaw thinking at that. I think we could call both those hon. members who sit on the front bench opposite the rickshaw twins from now on, because in their thinking they want to go back to the rickshaw.
By using machines you get more work done, and you get more pay. You take the drudgery out of the work. That is the aim of our western civilization. That is what we stand for. The standard of living in Canada depends on the productive efficiency of our industries and related services. The purpose of the proposed council is to stimulate this efficiency. Our products are sold in fierce competition on world markets, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) said, and if we lag behind our competitors in our methods or technologies we shall certainly lose those markets and our economy will decline. Jobs will be fewer, wages will be lower and there will be that degree of distress which hon. members opposite seem to think would be the best thing that could happen, from the way they have been talking.
I am glad the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) spoke. We have now heard three views on this question. That party was split with regard to the second reading; they could not agree how to vote. Two of its members are against any form of productivity, but the rest are for it. The hon. member for Peterborough says we have got to cure unemployment now, and that if we do not get these people back to work tomorrow we are no good.
All the members on the front bench on the other side have said that this bill will have no effect with regard to increasing employment. I do not know to what extent you have to spell out a measure. All I can say is that this lack of understanding must be due to the training, or lack of training, of members opposite. They should go to the people and find out what is happening. Productivity-the idea and philosophy behind it -represents a new step. It means that this is a joint effort by both workmen and management. The old idea was that management
Productivity Council
gave orders and the workers obeyed those orders. The more modern concept is that it is a co-operative affair. I would recommend to hon. members in the far corner of the chamber the words of Samuel Compers, the founder of the United States labour movement when he said that a company which did not make a profit was the worst enemy of the working man. New products mean expanded markets and greater trade. This is the background, and these are the objectives. This government has taken short term measures and it has taken intermediate measures to deal with this problem, but it is also the duty of a government to think ahead.
In spite of what the hon. member for Peterborough said-and this question is a rhetorical one; I do not want the hon. member for Essex East to answer it, because, of course, the answer is nothing-may I ask what measures did hon. gentlemen opposite bring forward when they first came to power? Mr. King did say "Not a five cent piece to help unemployment" though he qualified that by saying he would give five cents to provinces which had a Liberal government. What did they do about increasing aid to municipalities, about providing credits for exports, or aid to small business, or a winter works program, or the whole pantheon of constructive ideas which has been put forward by this government since it took office in 1957? This government has been a government of action. It has been a government which has done things. It has been a government of imagination; it has been a government that has won the confidence of the people, and it still has the confidence of the people.
I say that if hon. members on the other side cannot understand what this bill is about, then perhaps if they would go to some youth in the first year at high school he would try to tell them a few of the basic economic facts of life. I do not want to labour this too much. I suppose I should be taking the "more in sorrow than in anger" approach because the remarks which have been made on the other side are really pathetic. Hon. members over there just have not got any case; they have not got any ideas. That is why I say that this is rickshaw philosophy which has been brought forward-and I hope the hon. member for Essex East will not get to his feet on a point of order or a question of privilege; I expected it before this time, but I think it is strictly a good parliamentary description, and so those rickshaw twins had better get out of their rickshaws and get into the automobile age.

speechtext: We have not the exact figure, but it is estimated that some 2,560 jobs will be available for Indian people.

I think that this is an extremely important supplementary estimate, because the employment prospects as far as our Indian people are concerned have been few and far between in past years. Unfortunately, and perhaps by inadvertence, many of the Indian people have been prevented from obtaining an education, and this in itself makes it impossible for them to enter the employment field on the same basis as people who are not Indians. One reason why it is difficult for Indians to fit into our present day society, in some parts of Canada at least, is that we have in effect destroyed their economic system and foisted upon them our own concept of an economic system, which is one very different from the life they had originally known. We injected them into an employee-employer relationship in a wage structure economy without in any way preparing them to accept a change of that sort;

without giving them an educational background which might have fitted them for an economic structure of this type.
For this reason and others, the Indian population finds it extremely difficult to engage in employment except in very limited fields. For example, in the coastal region of British Columbia the Indian population is primarily engaged in the fishing industry. If the fishing industry is closed down, or when the season ends, the Indians find themselves with little possibility of additional employment. In effect, they have the opportunity of working part of the year in an industry which, to a certain extent, is connected with their traditional way of life in earlier years. They had to be good fishermen or they could not eat, so the transition in this regard is not too drastic. In recent years the logging industry has to a certain extent supplemented the income earned by fishing but even here the opportunities are extremely limited. It is my belief that we cannot think in terms of employment for Indians, that is, in the narrow sense as is reflected in this particular estimate, without keeping in mind the entire relationship of the Indian to the economic structure in which he has been forced to participate.
During the discussion of the bill which has just been passed concerning technical and vocational training I raised a question with the Minister of Labour having to do with the application of the principle contained in that measure to our native Indian people in so far as technical and training is concerned. The reply I received, and perhaps it was a correct one, was that that bill did not deal with Indians whose education comes wholly under the jurisdiction of the Indian affairs branch. Those Indians who attended provincial schools would, of course, receive the assistance made possible by the grants for vocational and technical training.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-ll, respecting procedure in relation to parliamentary divorce.

He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to thank the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) who seconded the motion for first reading, and also the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) for his support on second reading of this bill which I think can be of great assistance to us in solving a problem that has been before this house for many years.
This bill is likely to prove to be of great assistance to us in solving a problem which has been bothering the House of Commons for many years. The purpose of introducing it is to seek authority to permit such divorce actions to be tried by the Senate without reference to the House of Commons. I think it is a fair observation that the majority of our members on both sides of this house consider that the House of Commons should not be required to deal with divorce actions, for the following reasons. First, we are primarily a legislative body and we are not in a position to give proper judicial consideration to divorce actions. Second, the House of Commons has far too many national problems of greater importance than these individual actions. Therefore, in order to deal with individual divorce actions in a proper manner, if we are to act as a rubber stamp, we should be practical and logical; we should delegate our function relative to divorce matters to the Senate.
The same problem was encountered in the United Kingdom. They dealt with the question differently by means of the matrimonial causes act of 1857. Over a period of 150 years prior to that they dealt with 230 divorces, and apparently felt that these were too many to bother with. In other words, 230 divorces in 150 years were enough to stir the United Kingdom parliament into ridding itself of dealing with divorces. In Canada, 200 years later, we spend time dealing with more than 500 divorces each session. Either members of the Canadian parliament are more long-suffering or they have less regard for the true functions of parliament.
I think the time has come when we can deal with this matter realistically, in a way which will not offend the feelings of those who do not believe in divorce and, at the same time, provide relief to those who because of the laws of their province cannot obtain a divorce in the same manner as their fellow Canadians in other provinces.
It is suggested that each session we pass an act which will authorize the Senate to deal with all divorce cases during that session. The passing of this act will be a regular event; the house will not be divesting itself of its authority for an indefinite period. The effect of the act would automatically come to an end at the end of each session.
Parliamentary Divorce
There is precedent in the United Kingdom for one house alone dealing with a matter. The parliament act of 1911 in the United Kingdom, as amended by the parliament act of 1930, permitted, in the situation outlined in that act, the passing by the House of Commons of a bill on a certain number of occasions. If it were rejected by the House of Lords on a number of occasions, then the bill was passed on to receive the royal assent. So we have a precedent there.
I realize that this may not be the best way of dealing with the situation. It would be better if the problem were handed over to a special divorce court. However, we must be realistic. This cannot be done at the moment. The present proposal would be a first step; we in the House of Commons would delegate this power to the other place and then continue to study the whole matter. It might be objected that this bill will offend those who oppose divorce, especially in provinces which do not provide for divorce actions, but I would make the observation that there should be no more objection to this method of procedure than there is to passing on each application as it comes before this house.
Perhaps there may be some constitutional objection as regards section 55 of the British North America Act. But this is a question, really, of when royal assent may be given, and I feel that taking into consideration the rules of this house as set out in Beauchesne, especially paragraphs 6, 7 and 8 which state in effect that parliament is master of its own house, we can set our rules accordingly. I would point out that this involves private petitions, and that the house is in no way delegating its powers in respect of public matters. This involves people who come to us for relief, and we have on many occasions set up boards to deal with petitions of other types. As I said, this is a first step in the solution of this problem. The increasing number of applications for divorce places an unfair and unwarranted burden on the House of Commons, which has the responsibility for dealing with so many national problems during the time available. I appeal to the reasonableness of the members of this house, and to the moulders of public opinion, to exert their influence to the end that this house and, better still, this parliament shall be relieved of this task of dealing with divorce applications.

However, I think it can confidently be stated to this house that the other place will make certain changes in its procedure in order that an appeal procedure will exist. I think it is always very important that a parliamentary system of law should carry out a judicial process in a manner which provides the parties concerned with rights as close as possible to those which they would enjoy, for example, in provincial courts. I know of several cases-perhaps three-in the last half dozen years in which parliamentary divorce was granted and then it was found that the parties had not been served. There are also cases which plague provincial courts exercising divorce jurisdiction where exactly the same thing has happened.
This difficulty is known to the people in the other place. They continually revise their rules and do their best to deal with that most vexing problem and I think that we can safely entrust to them this chore. They know our views on this matter. They themselves are anxious to have things run properly. They are a fine group of people and are extremely conscientious about their work. I should not like to have left on the record any suggestion that they deal with it in a cavalier fashion.
